candidate_causes.cause_description: LV-101 (assumed V-001 liquid-outlet level control valve) failed to open on automatic demand due to a fault at the valve assembly (e.g., seized stem/trim, actuator or local air-supply fault, or positioner failure; mode undetermined), blocking liquid outflow.

evidence_against.relevance: Position feedback is the only indication of valve state, and a feedback-device fault would produce the same record. No stroke-test, flow or inspection data confirm physical closure or identify the failure mode.

evidence_for.relevance: An open command was issued while position feedback remained closed. This is the direct signature of a valve that did not stroke and explains the loss of liquid outflow. The record states LV-101 received the command, locating the fault at the valve.
LAH-102 and LAHH-103 both alarmed, corroborating a real, sustained accumulation consistent with a blocked liquid outlet.
No manual command to LV-101/LV-102 was recorded, so the open demand was automatic and correct in direction. The failure lies in the valve's response, not in the demand.

candidate_causes.cause_description: The open command was logged at the controller but not delivered to LV-101 (control output, I/O or signal-wiring fault), leaving the valve closed.

evidence_against.relevance: The record states LV-101 received the open command, which weighs against a delivery failure upstream of the valve. No comparison of controller output with valve input signal is provided.

evidence_for.relevance: A command/position discrepancy is also consistent with an open command that was logged but never reached the actuator.
A real, sustained high level is consistent with the valve physically remaining closed.

candidate_causes.cause_description: Restriction or blockage of the liquid outlet path downstream of LV-101, with LV-101 closed-position feedback erroneous (valve actually open).

evidence_against.relevance: Closed feedback already explains the loss of outflow. This hypothesis requires a coincident feedback-device failure (two independent faults), and no downstream pressure or flow data support it.

evidence_for.relevance: A sustained rise to the H and HH alarm points is consistent with any persistent outflow restriction, so this evidence does not discriminate.

candidate_causes.cause_description: Liquid inflow surge to V-001 exceeding outlet capacity as the primary cause. This requires LV-101 closed feedback to be erroneous; otherwise a surge could only be an initiating trigger.

evidence_against.relevance: With LV-101 remaining closed, normal inflow alone would produce the observed rise, so a surge is unnecessary as a primary cause and requires erroneous feedback. No inflow data are provided.

evidence_for.relevance: The automatic open demand shows level had risen above the controller set point. The source of that initial rise is not recorded and could be increased inflow.
Level reached both the LAH-102 and LAHH-103 points.

candidate_causes.cause_description: Malfunction or mispositioning of LV-102 (function and status not described in the packet) contributing to liquid accumulation.

evidence_against.relevance: The only recorded command/position discrepancy is on LV-101.
No manual command to LV-102 was recorded, excluding manual mispositioning within the available record.

evidence_for.relevance: LV-102 is named in the level-increase command record, indicating relevance to V-001 level control. Its position/feedback status is not reported, so involvement cannot be excluded.

candidate_causes.cause_description: Spurious high-level indication from a common-mode level-measurement error, with no genuine excess liquid.

evidence_against.relevance: Two separately tagged alarm points both activated, consistent with a genuine rise.
The level controller also demanded opening, a further concordant indication, and the valve failure provides a physical mechanism for real accumulation.
The record characterizes the event as a level increase.

evidence_for.relevance: Alarm records alone do not verify physical inventory, and independence of the control transmitter, LAH-102 and LAHH-103 is not confirmed.

candidate_causes.cause_description: Unrecorded operator action (manual closure or mis-operation of level valves or controller).

evidence_against.relevance: No manual command to LV-101 or LV-102 was recorded during the level increase.
An automatic open command was issued, showing the control system demanded the correct action. The fault was the valve's failure to respond.

evidence_for.relevance: No evidence in the packet supports an operator action. It is retained only as a residual hypothesis, bounded by the uncharacterized completeness of the command log.

parsed_response.concise_technical_rationale: HAZOP basis: Node V-001. The design intent (inferred, not stated) is to hold separator liquid level in its normal band by automatic control of LV-101. The deviation is MORE LEVEL (CASE-02). Evidence: E1 records an open command to LV-101 while position feedback stayed closed; this command/position discrepancy directly explains loss of liquid outflow. E3 shows LAH-102 and LAHH-103 both alarmed, corroborating a real, sustained accumulation. E2 shows no manual command to LV-101/LV-102, so the open demand was automatic and correct in direction. Most defensible cause (C1, 70%): LV-101 failed to open on demand due to a fault at the valve assembly (stem/trim, actuator, air supply or positioner; mode undetermined). A signal-delivery fault upstream of the valve (C2, 8%) is less likely because E1 states the valve received the command. Downstream restriction (C3) and inflow surge (C4) are less parsimonious because, as primary causes, they require the closed feedback to be erroneous at the same time. LV-102 involvement (C5) cannot be assessed. Spurious indication (C6) conflicts with concordant control and alarm indications. Operator error (C7) has no supporting record and is contradicted by E2 and by the automatic demand in E1. Consequences (CASE-03): flooding, liquid carryover to the gas line and treatment unit, possible generator damage, shutdown and production loss. Safeguards (CASE-04): LAH-102 and LAHH-103, both closing SDV-30010. The alarms functioned (E3), but SDV-30010 closure and timing are not evidenced, and both layers share one final element. Qualitative risk (no matrix supplied): consequence severity is high, the demand reached the HH layer and the final-element response is unverified, so this is high priority. Recommendations: stroke-test and inspect LV-101 (trim, actuator, air supply, positioner diagnostics) and compare controller output with the valve input signal. Retrieve alarm/trip records to confirm SDV-30010 closure and timing. Provide or verify an LV-101 command-versus-position discrepancy alarm. Confirm independence of LAHH-103 from LAH-102 and the control transmitter, and assess the shared SDV-30010 dependency. Inspect the gas line, treatment unit and generators for carryover effects. Review LV-101 maintenance and test history to establish the underlying root cause.
uncertainty_notes: The packet does not state LV-101's service. It is assumed to be the V-001 liquid-outlet level control valve, based on its tag and the open demand during rising level. The V-001 level design intent and set points are also not given.

Valve state is known only from position feedback. No outlet flow, controller-output trend, stroke-test, positioner-diagnostic, instrument-air or inspection data are provided, so the failure mode within C1 and the feedback-error alternatives (C3, C4) cannot be resolved.

E1 does not specify whether 'received an open command' means a signal verified at the valve or only the logged controller output. This limits discrimination between C1 and C2. C1 is typed mechanical as the dominant class, although it includes positioner and actuation faults.
The function and position/feedback status of LV-102 are not provided.
The completeness of the manual-command log is not characterized. Operator involvement is not inferred because no such action is recorded.

The packet does not state alarm timing and sequence, whether SDV-30010 closed, or whether carryover or generator damage occurred. The LAHH-103 alarm suggests the level continued past the LAH-102 point, but safeguard performance cannot be confirmed.
Independence of the level-control transmitter, LAH-102 and LAHH-103 is not confirmed. Both safeguards rely on the same final element (SDV-30010).
No maintenance, testing or failure history is supplied, so the underlying maintenance or organizational cause of the LV-101 failure cannot be determined.
The source possible-cause list is withheld (CASE-05), so the candidates and percentage allocations are independent qualitative judgments. No risk matrix was supplied, so risk ranking is qualitative.

I'm also weighing weaker alternatives: a downstream outlet restriction or blockage, which doesn't fully explain why the valve feedback showed closed, and an inflow surge exceeding outlet capacity, which similarly doesn't need the valve to be malfunctioning at all. Both of these get lower plausibility scores around 8% since the valve feedback data already sufficiently explains the level rise without invoking them, and there's no supporting inflow or downstream pressure data in the packet.

I'm now considering whether "received an open command" really confirms the command reached the valve itself, or just that it was issued from the controller — this distinction matters because a signal path failure (I/P converter, wiring, output card) between controller and actuator is a separate instrumentation/electrical cause from a purely mechanical valve/actuator failure like sticking or loss of air supply, so I want to split these into distinct candidate causes.

Since I can't distinguish the specific sub-mechanism from the evidence alone, it seems more defensible to group them under one primary cause — "LV-101 failed to stroke open on command (final control element failure)" — and list the mechanical, pneumatic, and signal-path possibilities as sub-causes under that umbrella rather than allocating separate percentages to each without stronger justification.
